output.answer: At the before air, nearest runs still recorded flames [bass-asrun-55] [bass-asrun-60]; near the after air, one recorded no ignition [bass-ii-o12], while another recorded an extinguished flame [bass-ii-o4]. output.whatChanges: No run sits exactly at the before air: closest result runs were at 22.6–22.7% oxygen, 8.3–8.4 points away, and recorded flames [bass-asrun-55] [bass-asrun-60]. At the after air, three runs sit there: one recorded no ignition and two have no stated result; the nearest stated-result run, 1.1 points higher at the same pressure, recorded no ignition [bass-ii-o12]. Runs 2.3–2.5 points higher recorded extinguished flames [bass-ii-o4] [bass-ii-b14] (outcomes read from notes). The app estimate changes from “Likely to burn,” 93% (90% range 79–100; high confidence), to “Likely to burn,” 90% (79–98; low confidence). The latter extrapolates below the lowest real test; both are estimates, not test results.
output.whatYouWouldSee: Before-air notes describe flames that persisted despite flow changes, though one got smaller at maximum flow [bass-asrun-55] [bass-asrun-60]. Less oxygen generally weakens flames, which may look smaller, dimmer, bluer and less sooty, but these after-air runs do not establish how this fabric fire would look.

output.instead: Runs recorded flames going out when airflow was reduced or turned off [bass-asrun-90-row100] [bass-asrun-110]. In microgravity, ventilation feeds the flame, so airflow control has more direct support here than relying on cabin oxygen reduction. A controlled test of this fabric at the after air and pressure, recording ignition and airflow changes, would address the evidence gap.
